title: External sandboxes for coding agents
body: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. README 節錄： # PyBot: can Python be a chatbot? LLMs drive today’s chatbots and agents, but chatbots long predate them. Sixty years ago, ELIZA held conversations by matching patterns in what the user typed and answering with predefined templates. It could seem insightful, but its repertoire was narrow, and expanding it meant writing more rules by hand. How far could a rule-based chatbot go if a swarm of agents did that work instead? We challenged a swarm of over 1,000 agents to build a chatbot entirely in Python: no weights, no training, just if-else branches, regex patterns and lookup tables. The agents wrote and evaluated over 5,000 versions, and the chatbot’s win rate on SmolTalkBench, where an LLM judge compares each reply with a reference answer, climbed from 0% to 26%. That puts it on par with SmolLM-360M-Instruct, which just a few years ago was state of the art for models under 1B parameters.
